I've farmed these 225 mu in Quzhou County for 15 years, and I know the wheat-maize rotation is what keeps this family fed. I'll put 200 mu into wheat-maize double cropping — that's the same 200 mu planted twice, winter wheat followed by summer maize. With only four people in the household and this much land, I can't do everything by hand. I rent a rotary tiller for the wheat and plant the summer maize no-till right after harvest, because the window between wheat coming off in early June and maize needing to go in is barely a week. There's no time to plow.

I have well irrigation, so I'll water the wheat three times this spring — green-up, jointing, and grain filling. Pumping costs money, but a dry spell at jointing costs me more in lost yield than the electricity bill. The extension office says 15 kg nitrogen per mu is enough for wheat, but from my experience, 20 kg gives me a steadier yield around 520 kg/mu. For the summer maize, I'll put down 18 kg N, 5 kg P, and 5 kg K per mu, irrigate twice, and expect about 580 kg/mu.

My 20 mu of chili is where I make my cash. It's labor-intensive, so I hire workers for transplanting and picking. I'll rotary till the plots, apply 20 kg N, 8 kg P, and 10 kg K per mu, irrigate five times, and spray pesticides five times because the aphids and diseases will ruin me otherwise. I expect about 1,600 kg per mu of fresh chili if the weather holds. The remaining 5 mu I keep in stevia for a local buyer who contracts with me every year. It's lower maintenance — 12 kg N, 5 kg P, 8 kg K, four irrigations, and two pesticide sprays — and should give me about 280 kg per mu of dried leaves. I always buy improved wheat seed and hybrid maize and chili seed. On a farm this size, saving seed is false economy.
